strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a conceptually simple recipe: use training dynamics to pair confident and unconfident examples, then supplement instruction tuning with hidden-state Mixup. It requires no additional human annotations or proprietary quality scoring.

The empirical coverage is substantial. Table 1 reports improvements across all seven model–dataset configurations, including three model families and datasets ranging from 52K to 939K examples. Healthcare experiments provide additional evidence, with average accuracy gains of 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points over NTP.

The human evaluation provides useful corroboration: across 200 judgments on 80 instructions, SFTMix receives 42.5% preference versus 26.5% for NTP, with 31% ties. This strengthens the evidence beyond automated judging alone.

Experiments with LoRA, data selection, smaller reference models, and multilingual tuning demonstrate practical flexibility within the tested settings. The paper also acknowledges the additional reference-model training cost.
weaknesses: The central claim that confidence-based pairing is crucial lacks the decisive control: ordinary random-pair Mixup on the same dataset with the same regularization settings. Section 5.2 changes the response data while testing quality-based pairing, so it does not isolate the benefit of confidence. Shuffled-confidence and single-checkpoint controls would establish whether training dynamics justify the added complexity. The distinction from the cited cartography-based Mixup work of Park and Caragea (2022) also needs clearer explanation.

Appendix A.1 selects hyperparameters using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, which are also the reported evaluation benchmarks; no independent development set is described. This introduces selection bias. Moreover, five evaluation rounds do not establish robustness across training seeds, and no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the generally modest gains. Transfer to healthcare is encouraging, but does not resolve these evaluation concerns.

The proposed mechanism is insufficiently demonstrated. A t-SNE visualization of extreme-confidence examples and a 7% reduction in confidence-score standard deviation do not establish reduced overfitting on confident examples or improved generalization on unconfident ones. The dispersion reduction could have several explanations. Section 3.4 establishes that Mixup generally changes gradients, without showing why that change produces the claimed benefits. Held-out, confidence-stratified analyses would provide stronger support.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful optimizer and training-schedule details. The manuscript provides no implementation link and leaves important choices unspecified, including reference-checkpoint timing, generation settings, exact judge versions, and LoRA configuration. The human study does not adequately describe annotators, assignment of judgments, response-order randomization, or agreement.

The practical cost–benefit case remains unquantified. SFTMix requires reference-model training and confidence estimation, yet there are no end-to-end runtime, memory, or compute-matched comparisons. The smaller-reference experiment supports feasibility, but does not establish the claimed suitability for constrained computation.

Several technical explanations need correction: the negative signs before cross-entropy in Sections 3.1 and 3.3 conflict with the cross-entropy gradient in Section 3.4; Section 5.3's distinction between an additional loss and regularization is simply a change in coefficient; and Beta(0.1, 0.1) concentrates near the endpoints rather than being flat. Overall, the consistent empirical improvements make Findings plausible, but the missing controls and evaluation/reproducibility gaps prevent a clear positive recommendation.
